slides.title: Basics of AI
slides.body: Know the tool before you lean on it. By the end of this class, you’ll have a prompt you wrote and a record of one claim you checked.

slides.title: Start with a question you care about
slides.body: Allow about 45 minutes. Think of a club task, a work shift or something you want to learn. A tool you’re already allowed to use is optional. Every exercise also works on paper.
slides.aria: Start with a question you care about

slides.title: What you’ll practice
slides.body: Explain how a chat tool produces text. Write a five-part prompt. Spot three kinds of error and check a claim. Decide what stays private. Use AI in ways your assignment allows.

slides.title: What stays in your hands
slides.body: Imagine planning a club meeting. A tool can draft an agenda. You decide the purpose, check the time and ask the advisor about room access. Those are three different jobs.

slides.title: What we mean by AI
slides.body: Here, AI means a chat tool that generates a response from instructions. A prompt is the text you give it. The model is the system producing the reply. Some tools also generate images or code.

slides.title: Where its authority ends
slides.body: A chat tool is software. It can write in the voice of a teacher without knowing what your teacher assigned. Even a detailed answer needs evidence before you rely on it.

slides.title: How a reply takes shape
slides.body: During training, a model learns patterns in examples. When you type a prompt, it uses those patterns and the conversation to predict likely pieces of text, one after another. That can produce a useful explanation.

slides.title: Why fluent answers can be wrong
slides.body: A real source title and a made-up title can both sound like something a textbook would cite. The model can produce a plausible sentence without having checked that the source exists.
slides.aria: Why fluent answers can be wrong

slides.title: Good tasks for a first try
slides.body: Ask for three ways to explain a concept, a quiz on notes you wrote, an order for meeting tasks, or different options to compare. Each gives you something you can inspect or practice.
slides.aria: Good tasks for a first try

slides.title: Watch for missing information
slides.body: A tool may repeat an old deadline, mix up two clubs or guess what a supervisor allows. It cannot infer a private rule you never supplied. Mark the missing detail and find the current source.

slides.title: Whose dress code is it?
slides.body: Ask “What is my school’s dress code?” A general reply may sound like policy. Find the current handbook or school website and read the relevant section. Ask school staff if the wording is unclear.

slides.title: You are the editor
slides.body: Circle a checkable statement in a draft, such as “the library closes at six.” Compare it with the posted hours for that day. Change or remove the statement if you cannot confirm it.

slides.title: Five parts of a useful prompt
slides.body: Task tells the tool what to do. Context supplies the facts. Constraints name the limits. Format describes what to return. Finish by asking it to flag uncertainty. Add a role only if it helps the task.
slides.aria: Five parts of a useful prompt

slides.title: A club agenda in 20 minutes
slides.body: “Write an agenda for my club” might yield welcome, updates and announcements. The stronger prompt below can yield 2 minutes to open, 7 for supplies, 6 for a rain plan and 5 for next steps. Check the sum and confirm who will lead each item.

slides.title: Rewrite a vague project request
slides.body: Start with “Help me with my group project.” Give the group a task, a deadline and a limit you know. Ask for an output you could use at your next meeting. Tell the tool how to handle facts it lacks.

slides.title: Practice check
slides.body: The next three questions check your judgment. Choose an answer on each slide and check your answers on the third. You can revisit any slide.

slides.title: Does a polished answer prove it’s true?
slides.body: Think of the difference between a clear explanation and evidence you can inspect.
slides.aria: Does a polished answer prove it’s true?

slides.title: Which instructions give useful boundaries?
slides.body: Look for the goal, the information the writer knows and the shape of the answer.

slides.title: Who can confirm a local rule?
slides.body: Think about where the rule was published and who can clarify it.
slides.aria: Who can confirm a local rule?

slides.title: Four ways a reply can mislead
slides.body: It might invent an article, reuse last year’s schedule, confuse two people with similar names, or agree with a mistaken assumption in your question. Ask yourself which kind of check each claim needs.
slides.aria: Four ways a reply can mislead

slides.title: Verify before you use it
slides.body: Open the primary source and find the passage that actually supports the claim. Try a practical step on a sample, or ask the person responsible. Leave anything you cannot verify out of work you share as fact.

slides.title: Catch a planted error
slides.body: Fictional AI error: “The U.S. Copyright Office requires every high school volunteer club to register its event flyers before posting them in a hallway.” An official name is no evidence. Look for the actual rule in agency guidance and the relevant school policy. This planted general requirement is unsupported. Discard it.

slides.title: What must stay out of a chat
slides.body: Keep passwords, one-time codes, national ID numbers, bank or card details, medical details, home addresses, API keys and login cookies out of prompts. A key or cookie can give someone access to an account.
slides.aria: What must stay out of a chat

slides.title: Protect other people’s information
slides.body: Use a fictional role in place of a roster, a friend’s situation or another student’s unpublished work. Tools may retain chats depending on their settings and policies. Read the current policy before sharing anything.

slides.title: Remove details the task doesn’t need
slides.body: Fictional overshare: “My friend Maya Hernandez, phone 555-0142, is free after 3:15 on Tuesdays at 412 Maple and needs help studying biology chapter 4.” Rewrite it with just the topic, study time and desired practice. Compare yours with the sample below.
slides.aria: Remove details the task doesn’t need

slides.title: Check account rules first
slides.body: Read the current terms for the exact app. If you’re under 18, use only tools you’re allowed to use and involve a parent or guardian when required. Use paper if needed. Never invent a birthdate or borrow an account to get around a limit.

slides.title: When AI can coach you
slides.body: If your teacher allows practice questions, answer a new practice question yourself. If a graded essay requires your own work, write it under those rules. Check teacher, professor or contest instructions and disclose AI help when required.

slides.title: When to close the chat
slides.body: Set it aside when an assessment bans AI or a task requires private data. Never use it to impersonate or harass someone. For a personal crisis or sensitive counseling need, reach out to a trusted adult or local support.

slides.title: Six prompts to keep
slides.body: Choose a prompt by the job you need done. Try explanation for learning, revision for your own draft, steps for planning, uncertainty for checking, comparison for decisions and prompt rewriting for a vague request. Remove personal details first.

slides.title: One prompt, one check
slides.body: Pick a non-graded task. Fill in the explain-and-quiz or flag-uncertainty prompt. Run it in an allowed tool or draft it on paper. Select one claim, check it against a source, and record what you found. If you have no answer yet, write the check you’ll run and mark it unverified.

slides.title: Would you use this answer?
slides.body: Explain it without reading the draft. Name the evidence for a claim you rely on. Check that you shared only necessary details and followed the rules. If any check fails, revise the draft or set it aside.

slides.title: Your prompt cheat sheet
slides.body: Keep the six prompts and your own practice notes. Try one prompt this week, remove private details and check one factual claim before using the answer.

slides.title: An optional completion record
slides.body: If you practiced the skill and pass the final quiz, you may keep a completion line. You choose whether it belongs on your profile.

slides.title: Final knowledge check
slides.body: Choose an answer on each of the next five slides. Four correct answers complete the class. After submitting, you can review the reasons and retry as often as you like.

slides.title: What does confidence prove?
slides.body: Judge the evidence behind the answer.

slides.title: Choose the strongest prompt
slides.body: Consider which request gives the tool useful facts, limits and a format.

slides.title: Which information stays private?
slides.body: Consider who owns each detail and whether it could expose an account or a person.

slides.title: Respect an assignment rule
slides.body: The instructions for this particular assignment govern how you may complete it.

slides.title: Before trying a new app
slides.body: Think about what you would check before creating an account.

slides.title: Five rules to take with you
slides.body: Fluent writing can be wrong. Give a complete prompt. Verify what you will use. Protect private data. Follow assignment and account rules. Review the reasons for your quiz answers below.
slides.aria: Five rules to take with you

slides.title: What comes next
slides.body: Brainstorming with AI takes the same prompt pattern into a decision. You’ll ask for more options, narrow them against constraints and choose one yourself.

slides.title: Your first strong prompt
slides.body: Follow the agenda walkthrough and check the time and roles yourself. The written script is available now.

slides.title: Practice without an account
slides.body: Write your prompt on paper. Trade a fictional example with a partner if allowed, or test it against the sample agenda here. Keep the prompt for a time when you have an allowed tool.

slides.title: Try one checked prompt this week
slides.body: Reopen your worksheet below to download a copy. Revisit the end quiz whenever you like. Completion records practice in this class and carries no school credit or certification.
slides.aria: Try one checked prompt this week

prompts.title: Explain, then quiz me
prompts.use: Learn a topic and practice recalling it.
prompts.text: Explain [TOPIC] to a first-time learner in plain language. Then ask me 5 short questions to check my understanding, one at a time. Wait for my answer before the next question. After each answer, tell me if I am right and why, without revealing the next question early. If you are unsure about a fact, say so and tell me how I could verify it. Do not invent sources.

prompts.title: Tighten this draft without adding facts
prompts.use: You wrote a draft and want clearer wording.
prompts.text:
Tighten the draft below. Keep my meaning. Do not add facts, numbers, titles, or claims I did not include. If something is unclear, ask me a question instead of guessing. Return: (1) the revised draft, (2) a short list of wording changes, (3) anything you were tempted to invent but did not.

DRAFT:
[PASTE YOUR DRAFT]

prompts.title: Break a task into steps
prompts.use: A project feels too big or vague.
prompts.text: Break this task into clear steps I can actually do. Task: [TASK]. Constraints: [TIME, TOOLS, WHAT I CANNOT DO]. Do not assume I have tools, money, or permissions I did not mention. Flag any step that depends on information you do not have. Format: a numbered list with the outcome of each step in one line.

prompts.title: Flag uncertainty
prompts.use: Separate what you know from what needs checking.
prompts.text:
Answer the question below. Separate your response into: (1) What you are reasonably confident about, (2) What you are unsure about, (3) What I should verify, and where a primary source might live. Do not invent citations. If you cannot answer, say so.

QUESTION:
[YOUR QUESTION]

prompts.title: Compare two options against my criteria
prompts.use: Compare options and make your own decision.
prompts.text:
Compare Option A and Option B only against the criteria I list. Do not pick a winner unless I ask. Do not invent extra criteria, costs, or facts. If a criterion cannot be judged from what I provided, say “not enough information.”

Option A: [A]
Option B: [B]
Criteria: [LIST]
Format: a short table, then 3 follow-up questions that would help me decide.

prompts.title: Rewrite my weak prompt
prompts.use: Your first request produced a generic answer.
prompts.text:
Rewrite my prompt so it includes a clear task, relevant context, constraints, an output format, and an instruction not to invent facts and to flag uncertainty. Ask me up to 3 questions if you still need information. Then output the improved prompt in a code block I can copy. Do not change my goal.

MY PROMPT:
[PASTE YOUR WEAK PROMPT]

prompts.title: A stronger club agenda prompt
prompts.use: Compare the limits with the weak request.
prompts.text:
Task: Draft a 20-minute agenda for a high school volunteer club meeting this week.
Context: We have 12 members, one advisor, and one event (a Saturday park cleanup) coming up in 16 days. We still need a supplies list and a rain plan. I will run the meeting.
Constraints: Do not invent club rules, budget numbers, or people who were not mentioned. Flag anything you are assuming. Keep it realistic for 20 minutes.
Format: A timed agenda with 4–6 items, each with a one-line purpose and who leads it (use roles, not made-up names).
If you are unsure about something, say so instead of filling the gap.

prompts.title: Safer study prompt
prompts.use: Compare after writing your own version.
prompts.text: Suggest a 30-minute study plan for a high school biology chapter on cells. The student has one weekday afternoon block and wants 10 minutes of practice questions at the end. Do not ask for personal contact details.

fields.label: What I verified, where I checked and what remains uncertain

reminders: Task + Context + Constraints + Format + Flag uncertainty.
Fluent writing can be wrong. Give a complete prompt. Verify before use. Protect private data. Follow school and account rules.
Never paste passwords, codes, IDs, financial or medical details, home addresses, keys, cookies, rosters or other people’s private information.
Use AI to explain or quiz when allowed. Do your own required work and disclose help when required.
Check the exact tool’s current terms. Under 18, involve a parent or guardian when required. Never bypass an age gate.

mid.prompt: What does a fluent answer fail to prove?
options: The content is true or complete.
The words form sentences.
Someone could edit the reply.
mid.why: Clear sentences can contain unsupported facts.

mid.prompt: Which prompt gives the clearest instructions?
options: Make a great plan.
Draft a 20-minute club agenda for 12 people. Use four timed items and flag unknowns.
You are brilliant. Help us.
mid.why: The goal, group size, limit and format guide the draft.

mid.prompt: Which question needs a local authority?
options: How can I group meeting ideas?
How could I structure a practice quiz?
What exact dress code does my school enforce today?
mid.why: Consult the current school policy. A model can help read a policy you supply but cannot set it.

final.prompt: A chat-based AI gives a smooth, confident answer. What does that confidence prove?
options: The facts have been checked against a primary source.
The answer is up to date.
Nothing by itself — the writing can sound sure and still be wrong.
The tool is allowed to be turned in as your schoolwork.
final.why: These tools generate fluent language. Tone is not a fact-check.

options: Tell me everything about leadership.
Make this impressive.
Draft a 20-minute volunteer-club agenda for 12 members with a cleanup in 16 days. Do not invent a budget. Use a timed list, and flag assumptions.
You are an expert. Give me the best answer.
final.why: It includes a task, context, a constraint, a format, and a request not to invent facts.

final.prompt: Which of the following should you never paste into an AI chat?
options: A made-up example about a student in a biology class.
A password, a one-time login code, or someone else’s phone number.
A public club event description you already posted on the school website.
A question about how to format a meeting agenda.
final.why: Secrets and other people’s private details do not belong in a prompt. A made-up example or already-public information is different.

final.prompt: Your teacher has banned AI on a graded essay. What is the honest move?
options: Have AI write the essay and rewrite a few words.
Follow the rule: do not use AI on that assignment; you may still use allowed study methods.
Use AI anyway if you do not get caught.
Use AI only for the citations, because citations are facts.
final.why: Honesty means following the rules that apply to that work. AI-written citations can also be wrong.

final.prompt: You are 16 and want to try a new AI app. What should you do first?
options: Invent a birthdate so you can sign up faster.
Use a parent’s account without asking.
Read that app’s current terms and age rules, and only use it if you are allowed — with a parent or guardian if the tool requires it.
Assume every AI tool has the same age rule as the last one you used.
final.why: Age rules differ by tool and can change. Use permitted tools and follow their rules.

steps: Read the weak request and the five parts of the stronger agenda prompt.
Add the draft’s time blocks and confirm the roles with the people involved.
Underline any invented permission or budget and remove it.
Save the prompt pattern and the check on your worksheet.
narration: A weak prompt sounds like this: ‘Write an agenda for my club.’ You’ll usually get something generic.
Here’s the same goal, written with a simple pattern: task, context, constraints, format, and a request to flag uncertainty.
I’m asking for a 20-minute agenda, for a 12-person volunteer club, with a cleanup in 16 days. I’m also saying: don’t invent a budget, and tell me what you’re assuming.
Watch how much more usable the draft becomes — and notice what I still have to do. I check the times. I confirm the roles. I don’t treat this as official club policy.

That is the habit this class is after: a clear prompt, then your judgment. If a sentence looks like a fact, you verify it before you use it. And you never paste passwords, IDs, or someone else’s private details just to get a better answer.
You’ll find this prompt pattern on your cheat sheet.
